routes.description: Establish that Bignon's experience, providentially interpreted coincidences, and supporting intellectual and historical considerations can jointly provide rational support for specifically Christian belief without compelling every observer.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the experiential pattern is rationally relevant under a comparative explanation, rival experiences do not neutralize it, and independent considerations can support its Christian interpretation at the modest standard of personal rational justification.

motionBridge.description: Show that the conversion experience and supporting considerations jointly make Christian belief rationally supportable despite naturalist and rival-religion alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Explain why the personally salient convergence of experiences and coincidences is more expected under providence than under an unaided naturalistic account.
Connect experience with intellectual considerations so the case supplies rational justification without requiring coercive or universally compelling proof.
Provide a principled way to distinguish the Christian interpretation from incompatible religious experiences through comparative intellectual and historical considerations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for why providential guidance in one conversion need not imply equivalent guidance or conversion opportunities for every person.
Clarify how surviving early Christian materials can aid access to historical claims without treating their abundance alone as proof of those claims.

routes.description: Establish that reverse conversions, culturally variable experiences, ordinary coincidence, and competing intellectual considerations remove any distinctive evidential advantage claimed for Bignon's Christian interpretation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic explanations adequately predict conversion patterns, rival experiences resist a uniquely Christian reading, and the proposed intellectual or historical adjudicators do not restore a clear evidential advantage.

motionBridge.description: Show that rival experiences and naturalistic explanations undercut the claimed evidential force of Bignon's experience for specifically Christian belief.

centralBridges.description: Explain how large populations, ordinary coincidence, and culturally familiar narratives can generate apparently coordinated conversion stories without providential causation.
Show how culturally diverse and directionally opposed religious experiences weaken an inference from personal experience to Christianity in particular.
Establish that philosophical and historical considerations remain contested and do not plainly break the symmetry between Christian, rival-religious, and naturalist interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether selective providential intervention fits the persistence of reasonable nonbelief and the uneven distribution of conversion experiences.
Distinguish evidential quality from documentary quantity by considering how institutional dominance and preservation affect the surviving record.

sections.title: Providential pattern or natural coincidence
sections.rationale: This section addresses the primary explanatory clash over whether the conversion story's coordinated and personally salient events favor divine providence or are expected among many lives shaped by ordinary coincidence and familiar narratives.

sections.title: Personal justification and the cumulative case
sections.rationale: This section fixes the relevant epistemic burden and examines how experience, philosophical argument, and background considerations may combine to support belief without forcing rational convergence or excluding reasonable disagreement.

sections.title: Rival religious experiences and Christian specificity
sections.rationale: This section tests whether culturally diverse experiences, reverse conversions, and disputed exceptions neutralize specifically Christian support, or whether different experiences can be compared without dismissing all experiential evidence.

sections.title: Historical and intellectual adjudication
sections.rationale: This section considers whether historical sources and broader intellectual arguments can adjudicate between Christianity and rival interpretations when experiential claims appear balanced, including the significance and limits of the surviving documentary record.

sections.title: Selective providence and persistent nonbelief
sections.rationale: This section examines whether a providential account of one person's conversion can accommodate uneven divine guidance, persistent reasonable nonbelief, and competing considerations concerning hiddenness without undermining the proposed explanation.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: After intellectual barriers weakened, Bignon's experience of guilt made Christian atonement intelligible and led to trust in Christ, relief from guilt, and perceived spiritual rebirth.
moves.attributionBasis: Bignon explicitly confirms the host's characterization and then gives a continuous first-person explanation of the experience and its religious interpretation.

response.rationale: This is a constructive account of how the guilt experience, atonement message, and resulting conversion fit together; it does not purport to answer an earlier locked move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly develops a central experiential component, though it offers limited comparative support for the interpretation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The first-person sequence and claimed experiential consequences are recoverable, with the spiritual-rebirth language clearly presented as Bignon's experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Certainty is confined principally to his own acceptance, relief, and perceived rebirth rather than being presented as public proof of Christianity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The experiential sequence is internally consistent, but the bridge from psychological relief to the truth of the Christian interpretation remains implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The first-person report specifically supports the occurrence and perceived effects, but it does not independently verify the theological explanation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly connects experience and Christian content to personal justification, placing it strongly within the cumulative-epistemology central tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage primarily narrates and interprets a first-person experience rather than assessing a live competing argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bignon states that the atonement message addressed his guilt, that he trusted Christ, and that the guilt evaporated with a perceived spiritual rebirth.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Conversion narratives run in opposing directions and can accompany reported improvements in values and meaning, so their existence alone supplies little net evidence for Christianity.
moves.attributionBasis: The host invites Oppy's assessment, and Oppy answers continuously by comparing familiar conversion patterns with stories of departure from Christianity.

components.text: Whether Bignon's conversion experience supplies evidential support for Christianity rather than merely reporting a personally transformative sequence.

response.rationale: Oppy contacts the evidential demand by introducing directionally opposed conversion stories and drawing the consequence that conversion narratives alone yield little net support.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full ordinary answers, it explicitly addresses the evidential inference from conversion and supplies a clear symmetry-based undercut.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly limited to the evidential value of conversion stories considered in both directions, rather than denying their sincerity or effects.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Oppy cautiously claims that opposing stories make the evidential result unclear and expressly avoids casting aspersions on participants.

charity.alternative: Bignon's conversion may contain distinctive details beyond the bare fact that a conversion occurred.
charity.decisiveQualification: Oppy's symmetry point here is expressly directed at the existence of conversion stories alone.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If relevantly similar transformation narratives run in contrary directions, their bare occurrence cannot straightforwardly discriminate among the incompatible conclusions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The general phenomenon of reverse narratives is specifically invoked, but prevalence, comparability, and representative examples remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the central experiential-diversity bridge by directly challenging Christianity-specific support from conversion testimony.

representationalCharity.rationale: He preserves the distinction between sincerity and evidential force, though this passage does not yet examine every distinctive detail in Bignon's account.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy explicitly notes stories of movement away from Christianity and says that stories in both directions complicate assessment of the total evidence.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Although a change of belief is weak evidence by itself, the coordinated and personally significant improbabilities in Bignon's story are more expected if Christianity is true than if atheism is true.
moves.attributionBasis: Bignon resumes in the first person after Oppy's challenge and explicitly distinguishes bare conversion testimony from the particular features of his own account.

components.text: Whether Bignon's case depends merely on the existence of a conversion narrative and is therefore neutralized by reverse-conversion stories.

response.rationale: Bignon concedes that bare belief change is weak evidence and distinguishes his case by appealing to coordinated, personally significant improbabilities under comparative hypotheses.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response explicitly contacts the symmetry premise and identifies the particular feature alleged to distinguish his case from bare conversion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition is clear and qualified, but 'improbable' is not tied to a specified probability model or reference class.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative claim is qualified, yet the asserted likelihood advantage exceeds what the unquantified examples alone establish.

charity.alternative: Reverse conversions can neutralize evidential force when the evidence consists only of conversion testimony.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon accepts that limited point and argues that his claimed evidence includes a distinctive pattern of events.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The likelihood comparison is a coherent reply, but it leaves implicit why these events are materially more expected under Christianity than under selection-rich naturalism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific incidents are named, but their base rates, independence, selection process, and likelihood under either hypothesis are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly maximally contacts the central experiential-pattern bridge by supplying the proposed comparative explanation of the coincidences.

representationalCharity.rationale: He accurately narrows Oppy's objection before presenting the alleged differentiator, without treating Oppy as denying every possible evidential distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bignon cites hitchhiking, hotel-location, and church-exit events and explicitly claims that these are more expected if Christianity is true than if atheism is true.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Across billions of lives, culturally familiar conversion scripts and ordinary coincidences can naturally generate apparently coordinated conversion stories without supernatural causation.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy takes the floor after Bignon's probabilistic claim, offers a counterexample, and then directly addresses the interpretation of the alleged improbabilities.

components.text: Whether the cited pattern of coincidences is genuinely less expected under naturalism than under a Christian providential hypothesis.

response.rationale: Oppy directly offers large-population opportunity, culturally familiar conversion scripts, and ordinary coincidence as a naturalistic explanation of the alleged pattern.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the likelihood comparison and supplies the principal alternative-generating mechanism rather than merely restating skepticism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The naturalistic mechanism is clear, though 'lots of people' and the range of relevant scripts and coincidences remain informally scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Oppy presents a plausible alternative interpretation rather than claiming deductive disproof, with uncertainty expressed through his point-of-view framing.

charity.alternative: Bignon's coincidences may be personally striking and could in principle receive a providential explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Personal salience does not by itself establish a likelihood advantage once population size, scripts, and selection are considered.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The population-and-script explanation coherently defeats an inference from subjective improbability unless independence and the relevant sampling process are established.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mechanisms are plausible and directly relevant, but the passage supplies no representative population data or quantitative base-rate comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central coincidence-naturalism bridge by explaining how apparently coordinated stories can arise without providential causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: Oppy treats the account as a genuine story while disputing its supernatural discrimination, though he does not quantify the residual improbability.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy identifies a familiar cultural conversion script, many people entering that script, and ordinary coincidences occurring along the way.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Even the strongest arguments on both sides fail to compel a unique verdict, leaving both theistic and atheistic positions rationally permissible.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy explicitly says Bignon has characterized his view accurately and immediately states his assessment of the aggregate arguments on both sides.

components.text: Whether the debate should require the experiential case to compel a unique verdict or instead assess whether belief remains rationally permissible.

response.rationale: Oppy expressly replaces a compulsion standard with aggregate assessment of the strongest arguments, preserving the rationality issue while allowing both positions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe is explicit and relevant to the epistemic standard, though it does not independently assess the particular likelihood claim about Bignon's events.

precisionFindings.rationale: The scope is clearly the aggregate arguments on both sides and the specific conclusion is noncompulsion rather than equal probability or truth.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that arguments do not compel is appropriately narrower than claiming that both worldviews have equal evidence or identical plausibility.

charity.alternative: A case can rationally support belief even when it does not compel every informed observer.
charity.decisiveQualification: Oppy's conclusion allows rational permissibility and denies only that the arguments force convergence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between rational permissibility and rational compulsion is coherent, although the move compresses the basis for permissibility on each side.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion rests on an asserted aggregate assessment without displaying the component arguments or explaining their comparative balance in this short span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central independent-balance bridge by fixing a nonconvergence conclusion, though it is less specific than later adjudication arguments.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage accurately preserves the modest pro standard and does not misrepresent rational support as requiring universal proof.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy agrees with the characterization of his view and says that even the best arguments, considered on both sides, do not compel a particular position.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: The converging improbabilities in Bignon's conversion story are well explained as providential acts intended by God to bring him to Christian faith.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly hands the conversation to Guillaume, who then narrates his conversion events continuously in the first person.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the positive providential explanation for the converging events and connects that explanation to their intended role in Bignon's conversion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves it clearly states the intended causal explanation, but it supplies little new comparative warrant against the naturalistic alternative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition, causal agent, intended end, and first-person justificatory scope are recoverable, with the explanation marked as Bignon's own assessment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrase 'quite well explained' is somewhat qualified, but the cited convergence does not itself establish strong comparative superiority over selection effects.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Providential intention can coherently unify the events, but explanatory compatibility is doing much of the work without a defended likelihood comparison.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion relies on personally salient coincidences and theological interpretation without establishing independence, base rates, or discriminatory predictive success.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the positive explanation required by the central experiential-pattern bridge and ties the convergence to providential purpose.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage principally constructs Bignon's providential account and does not substantially evaluate a live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bignon explicitly characterizes the improbabilities as well explained by God's providential control directed toward bringing him to faith.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Bignon's experiences need not compel an atheist in order to make his Christian conversion intellectually sensible and his resulting belief rationally permissible and personally justified.
moves.attributionBasis: Guillaume answers the host in the first person, describes the aims of his book, and explicitly addresses what Graham may reasonably grant.

components.text: Whether failure to compel atheists defeats the claim that Bignon's conversion can be intellectually sensible and personally justified.
Whether the naturalistic coincidence account must be disproved before Bignon can claim a personally rational interpretation.

response.rationale: Bignon directly accepts noncompulsion and argues for the narrower personal-justification standard; he does not answer the population-and-script mechanism itself.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer because it contacts the decisive epistemic-standard component while leaving the specific naturalistic explanation unaddressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The passage clearly distinguishes personal justification and permissibility from the stronger claim that atheism is irrational or that everyone must convert.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bignon deliberately limits the claimed achievement and acknowledges that the material need not establish the irrationality of atheism.

charity.alternative: Oppy's noncompulsion thesis may be correct even if Christian belief is rationally permissible for Bignon.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon accepts that thesis and claims only personal permissibility and intellectual sensibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from noncompulsion to compatibility with personal justification is explicit and coherent, with the ambitious universal conclusion expressly disclaimed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The modest epistemic conclusion fits the cited concessions, though this move does not itself establish that Bignon's underlying evidence meets a justification threshold.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly completes the central cumulative-epistemology step by articulating rational support without coercive proof.

representationalCharity.rationale: He accurately adopts the strongest modest interpretation of Oppy's position and does not inflate disagreement into a claim of atheistic irrationality.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bignon says he need not show atheism irrational and is satisfied with the claim that Christian belief may be justified, permissible, and sensible for him.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Persistent disagreement among expert philosophers of religion indicates that neither theistic nor atheistic arguments compel rational convergence, even after sustained inquiry.
moves.attributionBasis: The host addresses Graham immediately before this passage, and the speaker discusses professional philosophers from Oppy's characteristic first-person skeptical position.

components.text: Whether rationally serious inquiry should be expected to compel convergence beyond the modest standard of personal permissibility.

response.rationale: Oppy supports the noncompulsion position by pointing to persistent disagreement among philosophers who have devoted sustained attention to the relevant arguments.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supports nonconvergence, but expert disagreement is indirect evidence and does not test the quality of Bignon's personal justification in detail.

precisionFindings.rationale: The nonconvergence point is clear, though the relevant expert population and what counts as sustained inquiry are informally bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Oppy treats disagreement as making compelling one-sided arguments unlikely, not as proving that no side has any evidential advantage.

charity.alternative: Experts may disagree even when one position has better arguments or when some participants reason imperfectly.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move supports absence of compulsion, not equality of evidence or universal expert reliability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Persistent informed disagreement is relevant to noncompulsion, but the inference requires an implicit premise about expertise, independence, and adequate access to evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A recognizable pattern of professional disagreement is identified, but no distributional data or controls for specialization and dependence are supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central independent-balance bridge, although it is an indirect indicator rather than a comparison of the arguments themselves.

representationalCharity.rationale: The restrained conclusion avoids the strongest crude appeal to authority, though the inference still depends on assumptions about the expert distribution.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy points to the continued presence of both theists and atheists among philosophers of religion after extensive professional engagement.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Naturalism has a structurally parallel cumulative case, while arguments from evil and divine hiddenness require theists to identify which premises they reject and accept the resulting commitments.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker refers to a case for naturalism developed in his own works and then explicitly describes theists as the opposing audience evaluating it.

components.text: Whether a cumulative Christian case can claim rational support without also confronting a structurally parallel naturalist case and major contrary arguments.
Whether selective providential action is compatible with the evidential force of evil and divine hiddenness.

response.rationale: Oppy contacts the cumulative-case demand by identifying a parallel naturalist case and requires explicit premise-level engagement with evil and hiddenness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts both cumulative balance and hiddenness, but it mostly sets a burden of analysis rather than executing the comparative analysis in this span.

precisionFindings.rationale: The naturalist parallel and the premise-rejection demand are recoverable, though the contents of the naturalist case are only referenced rather than specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Requiring theists to identify rejected premises and commitments is proportionate as a dialectical requirement, while no decisive refutation is asserted.

charity.alternative: Theists can rationally reject premises in arguments from evil or hiddenness without having a complete public refutation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Oppy asks them to identify those premises and resulting commitments rather than assuming that rejection is unavailable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The symmetry and premise-commitment points are coherent, although the conclusion remains programmatic without the underlying naturalist case being developed here.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Serious contrary argument families are specifically named, but their premises, empirical support, and comparative force are not presented in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports central independent balance by requiring the cumulative Christian case to account for substantial naturalist counterevidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly frames the theist's task at the premise level and avoids treating the existence of evil or hiddenness arguments as automatic disproof.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy invokes his cumulative case for naturalism and specifically identifies evil and divine hiddenness as arguments requiring premise-level theistic responses.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Christian providence need not imply that God tries maximally to convert everyone, because God may have morally sufficient reasons for saving some people and not others.
moves.attributionBasis: The first-person speaker identifies his Calvinist view and his own work on free will and divine providence, clearly marking Guillaume's response.

components.text: Whether providential guidance of Bignon is inconsistent with uneven conversion, persistent nonbelief, and the hiddenness-related challenge.

response.rationale: Bignon directly denies that providence entails maximal divine effort to convert everyone and invokes morally sufficient reasons for selective salvation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive consistency challenge is contacted, but the asserted morally sufficient reasons are not identified or defended, leaving the answer materially incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The Calvinist scope and modal conclusion of consistency are clear, but the content of the alleged morally sufficient reasons remains unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is framed as consistency and acknowledges that puzzles remain, appropriately avoiding the stronger claim that hiddenness has been fully explained.

charity.alternative: Selective providence creates a genuine puzzle about why reasonable nonbelief and unequal conversion opportunities persist.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon acknowledges the puzzle while denying that universal maximal conversion effort follows from his Calvinist view.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Bare consistency is possible, but the unsupported conditional that God has sufficient reasons leaves the substantive hiddenness challenge unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No particular moral reason or independent support is supplied; the central explanatory work is performed by an asserted possibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly contacts the subsidiary selective-providence bridge and offers the relevant consistency response, albeit in underdeveloped form.

representationalCharity.rationale: He recognizes the opposing concern rather than dismissing it, though invocation of unspecified reasons does not resolve its strongest evidential form.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bignon identifies his Calvinist view, denies that God must try maximally to convert everyone, and asserts morally sufficient reasons while acknowledging remaining puzzles.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The cultural and historical diversity of religious experiences and their interpretations substantially weakens testimonial support for Christianity specifically.
moves.attributionBasis: The host asks Graham which concern matters, and the response develops Oppy's skeptical argument using culturally specific Australian religious testimony.

components.text: Whether religious experience can specifically justify Christian interpretation once culturally and historically divergent experiences are considered.
Whether uneven religious interpretation is adequately explained by selective providence or instead reflects cultural dependence.

response.rationale: Oppy directly develops cultural and historical diversity as an undercutter of Christianity-specific testimonial force but does not engage Bignon's Calvinist explanation of selectivity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It strongly contacts experiential specificity while leaving the separate selective-providence rationale unanswered, making the overall response partial.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument concerns Christianity-specific evidential value of testimony after learning its cultural history, not the impossibility of all religious experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that diversity makes specific testimony difficult to credit is qualified and supported by a concrete historical-cultural contrast.

charity.alternative: Culturally shaped interpretation does not entail that every religious experience is false or evidentially worthless.
charity.decisiveQualification: Oppy argues that diversity weakens Christianity-specific testimony, not that cultural mediation proves universal falsity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Cultural dependence and incompatible interpretations coherently undercut a straightforward inference from testimony to Christianity unless an adjudicator is supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete temporal and cultural example supports the mechanism, though broader representativeness and comparative testimony rates remain undocumented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly maximally supports the central experiential-diversity bridge by directly explaining why testimony does not uniquely favor Christianity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument preserves the distinction between undercutting specificity and dismissing every experience, while using cultural variation as the relevant defeater.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy cites diversity in interpretations and the absence of specifically Jesus-directed testimony in pre-Christian Australian cultural settings.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Non-Christian religious experiences may count against naturalism without supporting Christianity, while unreliable practices can be rejected case by case without thereby discrediting Bignon's experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly invites Guillaume's answer, and the speaker cites Ken Pearce, agrees selectively with Oppy, and contrasts dubious practices with his own experience.

components.text: Whether non-Christian and culturally diverse religious experiences neutralize Bignon's Christian experience or can be assessed differentially.
Whether all directionally opposed experiences possess equal evidential status merely because they are reported.

response.rationale: Bignon directly distinguishes evidence against naturalism from evidence for Christianity and proposes case-by-case rejection of unreliable practices and interpretations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive diversity and symmetry demands, but the criteria for identifying unreliable practices and mistaken interpretations remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The differential framework is clear, but 'unreliable practices' and adequate theological explanation lack specified assessment criteria.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers a possible differentiated treatment rather than claiming that all non-Christian cases have already been successfully explained away.

charity.alternative: Religious diversity may undercut Christianity even if some non-Christian experiences also count against naturalism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bignon must still justify his case-by-case classifications and the specifically Christian inference from his own experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The three-way distinction is coherent, but without principled reliability criteria it risks insulating favored experiences through case-specific judgments.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The framework is attributed to a philosophical proposal, yet the passage supplies little representative evidence or defended application to actual rival cases.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports central rival adjudication by resisting blanket parity, though it does not yet provide a sufficiently operational comparative method.

representationalCharity.rationale: He grants evidential force to some rival experiences instead of dismissing them wholesale, though his proposed differentiators remain underdeveloped.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bignon says some non-Christian experiences may undermine naturalism, while theological interpretation and unreliable practices must be assessed separately from his own case.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: Preferring a Christian interpretation of religious experience is not special pleading if Christianity and Bignon's conversion possess stronger supporting reasons than rival claims.
moves.attributionBasis: The host directs the special-pleading question to Guillaume, whose first-person defense follows continuously before Graham begins a new challenge.

components.text: Whether preferring the Christian interpretation amid diverse religious claims is arbitrary special pleading or rests on comparative reasons.

response.rationale: Bignon directly states the condition under which special pleading would arise and claims that unequal comparative reasons distinguish his Christian preference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the accusation's decisive criterion, but the better reasons are asserted rather than exhibited, so the substantive answer is partial.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional account of special pleading and the claimed domain of better reasons are clear, with no material shift between personal and general preference.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bignon frames the point as his considered view, but claims better Christian reasons without presenting enough comparison in this passage to support that force.

charity.alternative: Even sincere confidence in better reasons can be special pleading if rival evidence is assessed asymmetrically.
charity.decisiveQualification: Avoiding special pleading requires demonstrated comparative standards, not merely the assertion that reasons are unequal.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional principle is sound, but the inference to his case depends on the undeveloped premise that his Christian reasons are actually stronger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The decisive comparative premise is asserted without examples, independent criteria, or evaluation of the strongest rival reasons in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly reaches central rival adjudication by proposing comparative reasons as the discriminator, despite weak execution of the comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: He identifies the correct need for comparative reasons but does not engage the strongest concern about asymmetric assessment of those reasons.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bignon says special pleading would require equal or absent reasons and asserts that he has better reasons for Christianity and his Christian interpretation.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: When Christian and Muslim religious experiences appear comparable, historical and intellectual evidence concerning Muhammad, Jesus, and the resurrection can adjudicate between their incompatible interpretations.
moves.attributionBasis: The host asks Guillaume how to decide between equally compelling experiences, and Guillaume answers by proposing comparison of historical evidence.

components.text: How incompatible but phenomenologically comparable Christian and Muslim experiences can be adjudicated without arbitrary preference.
Whether historical and intellectual evidence can supply discrimination even when experience alone does not compel convergence.

response.rationale: Bignon directly proposes independent historical and intellectual evidence concerning Muhammad, Jesus, and resurrection as the referee when experience ties.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly supplies the requested type of adjudicator, though its actual comparative result is asserted more than demonstrated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The tie condition, proposed referees, and comparative conclusion are clearly recoverable, with experience alone expressly treated as insufficient.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bignon acknowledges his Christian standpoint, but the strong claimed evidential superiority is not established by the brief list of historical topics.

charity.alternative: Comparable Muslim experience can remain evidentially live even if Christianity has an independent historical case.
charity.decisiveQualification: The historical and intellectual evidence must be independently assessed rather than presuming the Christian result.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Using evidence independent of the tied experiences is a coherent method for breaking symmetry, with only the execution of the comparison left open.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Relevant domains are named, but no source analysis or resurrection warrant is provided to establish that Christianity is actually stronger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and nearly completely states the method required by the central rival-adjudication bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: He accepts the experiential tie for purposes of analysis and seeks independent adjudication, though his confidence in the result outruns the displayed comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bignon proposes comparing sources about Muhammad and Jesus and assessing the resurrection argument when Christian and Muslim experiences appear tied.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Comparative assessment of Christianity and Islam requires substantial expertise, and the available historical record does not plainly establish a stronger case for Christianity.
moves.attributionBasis: The host addresses Graham, who answers with first-person cautions about his expertise and then compares the historical records of Islam and Christianity.

components.text: Whether comparative historical evidence plainly breaks the experiential tie in Christianity's favor.
Whether the claimed better reasons for Christianity have been established through competent comparative assessment.

response.rationale: Oppy directly disputes a clear Christian historical advantage, stresses the expertise required, and identifies richer early information for Islam as a counterconsideration.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly contacts both the proposed historical referee and the claimed comparative superiority with a concrete countercomparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: Oppy limits the conclusion to absence of a plain historical advantage and explicitly conditions the comparison on what one is trying to authenticate.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cautionary force is proportionate: he does not claim Islam true, only that recency and source access complicate Christian superiority.

charity.alternative: Christianity might have stronger evidence for particular claims even if Islam has a more recent and fuller institutional record.
charity.decisiveQualification: Comparative strength depends on the precise claim being authenticated and cannot be inferred from a generic historical comparison.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The claim-specific and expertise cautions validly block a simple inference to Christian superiority, while allowing that narrower comparisons might differ.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The recency and early-cultural-record comparison is concrete, but the passage does not systematically compare source quality for the contested religious claims.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports central independent balance by directly challenging the proposed historical tie-breaker's alleged Christian result.

representationalCharity.rationale: Oppy expressly includes the claim-specific qualification and avoids treating documentary recency as automatically settling religious truth.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy notes greater chronological proximity and knowledge concerning early Islam and cautions that evidential strength depends on the particular claim being authenticated.

moves.speaker: Guillaume Bignon
moves.proposition: The quality, quantity, and tested historical reliability of New Testament sources provide Christianity with stronger historical support than Islam after careful comparison.
moves.attributionBasis: Guillaume identifies his own limited expertise but then presents the Christian apologetic case, contrasting New Testament and Quranic source reliability.

components.text: Whether Christianity lacks a clear comparative historical advantage over Islam once source quality and reliability are considered.

response.rationale: Bignon directly counters with claimed advantages in source quality, document quantity, geographical detail, names, and tested New Testament reliability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response contacts the comparative challenge with specific criteria, but relies substantially on expert attribution and undeveloped reliability claims.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criteria are identifiable, but 'quality,' 'reliability,' and 'well tested' are not operationalized for the supernatural claims at issue.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Christianity's larger surviving documentary record partly reflects later institutional dominance and selective preservation, so document quantity alone is not compelling evidence of historical superiority.
moves.attributionBasis: Graham explicitly returns to an earlier caution and explains how copying, preservation, and destruction practices shaped the surviving documentary record.

components.text: Whether the greater quantity of surviving Christian documents independently demonstrates superior historical support.
Whether source quality and claim-specific reliability, apart from quantity, establish Christian superiority.

response.rationale: Oppy directly undercuts document quantity through institutional copying, preservation, and destruction effects but does not answer Bignon's separate quality and reliability claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer because it directly defeats the quantity component while leaving the source-quality component substantially untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is expressly limited to the argument from weight of documentation and does not claim that every Christian document is unreliable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The institutional-selection mechanism appropriately supports the bounded conclusion that quantity alone is not compelling evidence.

charity.alternative: A large documentary record can still be evidentially useful even when preservation was institutionally selective.
charity.decisiveQualification: Selective survival defeats quantity as an independent proxy for truth but does not erase claim-specific source quality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Institutional dominance affecting copying, preservation, and destruction directly undermines a simple inference from surviving quantity to historical superiority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific preservation mechanisms are identified, though their magnitude and exact comparative impact on Christian and Islamic corpora are not documented here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly maximally supports the subsidiary source-survival bridge by distinguishing preserved quantity from evidential quality.
